source_text: Et occulta tenebrarum ipse inluminabit, utique per Christum, qui Christum in lumen nationum repromisit quique se lucernam pronuntiauit scrutantem renes et corda. ab illo erit et laus unicuique, a quo et contrarium laudis, ut a iudice. certe, inquis, uel hic mundum deum mundi interpretatur dicendo: spectaculum facti sumus mundo, et angelis et hominibus, quia, si mundum homines mundi significasset, non etiam homines postmodum nominasset. immo, ne ita argumentareris, prouidentia spiritus sancti demonstrauit, quomodo dixisset: spectaculum facti sumus mundo, dum angelis, qui mundo ministrant, et hominibus, quibus ministrant. uerebatur nimirum tantae constantiae uir, ne dicam spiritus sanctus, praesertim ad filios scribens, quos in euangelio generauerat, libere deum mundi nominare, aduersus <quem) nisi exerte non posset uideri praedicare.
pass_a_gloss: And He Himself will illuminate the hidden things of darkness, certainly through Christ, who promised Christ as a light to the nations and who declared Himself a lamp examining kidneys and hearts. From Him will be praise for each one, and from Him also the opposite of praise, so that from the judge. Certainly, you say, or does this God of the world interpret, saying: we have been made a spectacle to the world, and to angels and to men, because, if he had meant the world of men, he would not have named men afterwards. On the contrary, lest you argue thus, the providence of the Holy Spirit demonstrated how he spoke: we have been made a spectacle to the world, while to angels, who minister to the world, and to men, to whom they minister. For the man of such great constancy, or rather the Holy Spirit, feared, especially when writing to the sons, whom he generated in the gospel, to freely name the God of the world, against whom, unless openly, he could not be seen to preach.

pass_b_english: Through Christ, God Himself will shed light on the darkest secrets, for Christ is the light that God promised to the nations, and He's the one who examines the deepest recesses of our hearts. It's from God that we'll receive either praise or criticism, depending on how we stand before Him as our judge. You might argue that the phrase 'God of the world' refers to the God who created the universe, citing the phrase 'we have become a spectacle to the world, to angels, and to humans.' But if that were the case, wouldn't it be redundant to mention humans separately, implying that 'the world' already includes them? The Holy Spirit, however, intentionally worded it this way to make a point: we're on display to the world, but more specifically, to the angels who serve the world and to the humans they serve. The writer, driven by the Holy Spirit, was cautious not to explicitly mention the 'God of the world' when writing to his spiritual sons, born through the gospel, because he wanted to make it clear that he was preaching against this false god, and he couldn't do that without being overt about it.

review.notes: Pass B introduces significant interpretive additions and shifts in agency/meaning that contradict the Locked Latin and Pass A. 1. Pass B claims 'Christ is the light that God promised', whereas the Latin 'qui Christum in lumen nationum repromisit' (and Pass A) indicates Christ is the one who promised Christ (or the promise of Christ) as a light. 2. Pass B interprets 'renes et corda' as 'deepest recesses of our hearts', whereas the Latin and Pass A correctly identify 'kidneys and hearts'. 3. Pass B adds 'depending on how we stand before Him', which is an interpretive expansion of 'ut a iudice'. 4. Pass B interprets 'deum mundi' as 'the God who created the universe', whereas the context of the argument (and the Latin) is about the 'God of the world' (a title Tertullian is critiquing). 5. Pass B changes the meaning of the final clause: the Latin 'ne dicam spiritus sanctus... libere deum mundi nominare, aduersus quem... non posset uideri praedicare' suggests the Holy Spirit was *cautious* or *seemed hesitant* to name the God of the world freely because he was preaching against him; Pass B turns this into a positive intention: 'The Holy Spirit, however, intentionally worded it this way... because he wanted to make it clear'.
reasons: Pass B contradicts the Latin agency and meaning in the first sentence: 'qui Christum in lumen nationum repromisit' (who promised Christ as a light to the nations) is rendered as 'Christ is the light that God promised', which changes the subject of the promise.

Pass B contradicts the Latin in the final sentence: 'ne dicam spiritus sanctus... libere deum mundi nominare' (lest I say the Holy Spirit... freely name the God of the world) is rendered as 'The Holy Spirit, however, intentionally worded it this way... because he wanted to make it clear', which reverses the sense of the Spirit's perceived caution/hesitation described in the Latin.
